html:
The Iñupiat (singular Iñupiaq) are the Inuit of northern and northwestern Alaska. Their land runs from Norton Sound on the Bering Sea north and east along the Arctic coast to the Canadian border.

They descend from the Thule culture, which took shape in northern Alaska around 1000. Thule people hunted bowhead whales from large skin boats called umiaks, and from Alaska they spread east across the Arctic to Greenland in the Thule migration. So the Iñupiat are close kin of the Inuit of Canada and Greenland, and neighbours of the Yupik to the south.

Coastal villages lived from whales, walrus and seals; inland groups followed caribou herds. Trade fairs linked them with Siberia across the Bering Strait.

European whalers and traders arrived in the 1800s, bringing disease and alcohol. After the sale of Alaska to the United States, the discovery of oil at Prudhoe Bay pushed through the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act of 1971, which set up Native corporations such as the Arctic Slope Regional Corporation.
sum: The Iñupiat (singular Iñupiaq) are the Inuit of northern and northwestern Alaska. Their land runs from Norton Sound on the Bering Sea north and east along the Arctic coast to the Canadian border.
